props.title: Drunken Master
props.initialSlug: Jackie Chan masters kung fu through boozy training

sections.content: Drunken Master revolutionized martial arts comedy and launched Jackie Chan's signature style. Chan plays Wong Fei-hung, a troublemaking student who masters the unpredictable "drunken fist" technique under harsh mentor Beggar So (Yuen Siu-tien). The film's brilliance lies in how it transforms traditional kung fu training sequences into slapstick gold while showcasing legitimately impressive martial arts. This marked a decisive shift from the serious tone of Bruce Lee films like Enter the Dragon (1973), establishing a new template for action-comedy that influenced everything from Police Story (1985) to Rumble in the Bronx (1995).

sections.content: Director Yuen Woo-ping's influence cannot be overstated. His choreography in Drunken Master pioneered a more acrobatic, comedy-influenced style that would later attract Hollywood - he went on to choreograph The Matrix (1999) and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000). The film's training sequences, particularly the "ladder of pain" and "hot coal" scenes, created a template for mixing physical comedy with genuine martial arts skill that's still referenced today in films like Kung Fu Hustle (2004) and The Forbidden Kingdom (2008).

The film's technical innovations were groundbreaking for 1978. The camera movement during fight scenes, with its dynamic tracking shots and creative angles, influenced countless martial arts films that followed. While earlier kung fu films like Five Fingers of Death (1972) used relatively static wide shots, Drunken Master's cinematography got up close to the action, establishing techniques that would become standard in modern action filmmaking from Ong-Bak (2003) to The Raid (2011). sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond martial arts cinema. Its combination of physical comedy and action created a template that influenced Hollywood blockbusters like Rush Hour (1998) and Shanghai Noon (2000). The "drunken" fighting style itself has appeared in numerous video games and films, from The Last Dragon (1985) to The Forbidden Kingdom (2008), showing how this single film helped create an entirely new martial arts subgenre.
